item.title: Trump's midterm deadline has the Middle East bracing for another round of war
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Black smoke and flames rise from an oil facility in an industrial area in southern Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, which has found itself under attack from the Iran-allied Houthis. - STR/AP With little transparency from Washington and warmongering from Tehran, people across the Middle East have been left anxious and confused, scanning for signals on whether the conflict between Iran and the United States will reignite. “The mood has definitely shifted,” a 36-year-old American national living in Saudi Arabia told CNN. She plans to leave before Tuesday’s midterms, after which US President Donald Trump has hinted renewed fighting is possible. “People are more cautious in general, and it feels like a waiting game to see what happens,” she added. At home and workplaces across Gulf Arab countries, questions are swirling. Residents are searching for clues that could help them make plans in case of school closures or travel disruption. The war began in February when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. It entered its eighth month this week with both sides still locked in a stubborn stalemate, neither making progress diplomatically nor capable of breaking the military impasse. Trump has offered little clarity on his endgame, oscillating between threats of further strikes and openness to possible diplomacy. Iran has tried to project its own deterrence, claiming it now possesses weaponry capable of striking more targets and inflicting even greater damage than before. Mediation is continuing – but a breakthrough would depend on at least one of the two sides breaching their own red lines. Trump wrote on social media earlier this month that Washington “will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections.” That the US president neither ruled out or confirmed strikes would resume afterwards is part of the reason for the ongoing nerves. “The US has been actively feeding into this regionwide sense of anxiety as it keeps signaling that another round of escalation might be imminent” Hasan Alhasan a senior fellow for Middle East policy at the International Institute for Strategic Studies told CNN. “But it’s becoming difficult to distinguish pressure tactics from genuine signals.” Adding to a sense that escalation could be imminent, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - who partnered the US in attacking Iran and has been pushing for new strikes - will remain in office despite losing his majority in the recent elections. Negotiations to form a new government in Israel look set to begin in earnest next week, but election results suggest it will be difficult for opposition parties to oust Netanyahu quickly, if at all. Benjamin Netanyahu lost support in Israel's election but for now, remains prime minister. - Bloomberg/Bloomberg/Bloomberg via Getty Images In the absence of clarity, residents in the region often rely on hearsay or search social media for reports on troop movements to determine whether a US strike is imminent. Over the past month, Iranian military commanders have also intensified a series of public messages claiming that Iran has built-up large stockpiles of new weapons, a tactic designed to induce fear among Washington’s allies in the region. A senior security official in Tehran told CNN that Iran will try to target infrastructure beyond oil facilities in the region, including AI, and warned that if the conflict resumes, it will be a long “war of surprises.” On Saturday, Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered a response “without geographical limitations” to any new threat, an apparent effort to present a leader still yet to be seen in public as playing an active role in military preparations. Foreign workers drawn to wealthy Gulf Arab states by economic opportunities and a tax-free lifestyle have for decades lived in relative stability in a region mired in conflict. That sense of security was shattered this year after the US and Israel launched the war, prompting Tehran to fire unprecedented barrages of ballistic missiles and drones onto Arab cities disrupting schools, travel and business and causing multiple casualties. Yet despite the war, many residents stayed put, telling CNN they feel confident under the protection of well-armed regional militaries. Practical concerns remain, though. “I’m actively trying not to think about that happening again because I really don’t want another winter with strikes,” Michelle, a 36-year-old American resident in Abu Dhabi told CNN. “I’ve always felt safe here…but I’m more concerned that our lives will have to change again.” This month, people were surprised to find out that families of US diplomats have begun discreetly leaving, with the sudden departures becoming known only after their children started saying goodbye to classmates at school. Many of those leaving had only recently returned to their posts after being ordered out at the height of the Iran war in March, making the exits feel like a frustrating and chaotic déjà vu. Iran attacked Qatar in the conflict but the country is performing a key mediating role. - Mahmud Hams/AFP/Getty Images Fueling anxiety among residents are reports of thousands of US troops being dispatched to the region , as reported by the Associated Press. In Saudi Arabia, where major events have already been canceled and offices closed with staff working remotely after the Iran-allied Houthi rebels intensified strikes, residents told CNN the were concerned that a return to war could increase pressure on a country already embroiled in conflict along its southern border. “My neighbors and friends are bunkering for November but starting to get concerned about flights disruptions over the holidays,” said the 36-year-old American national in Saudi Arabia, comparing it to the covid era. “A lot of offices have moved to virtual or have reduced staff and remote learning is in place.” Elsewhere in the region, other international gatherings remain on track, though the risk remains that they could be disrupted if the US launches strikes in the coming week. In Abu Dhabi, where no attacks have been recorded since May, two US oil firms canceled plans for their executives to attend one of the region’s biggest oil conferences citing security concerns, Reuters reported. The event will proceed as scheduled next week with “strong” US participation and more than 120 American exhibiting companies, the organizer, DMG, told Reuters. The conference is expected to host nearly 240,000 people, according to the organizers. In Bahrain, one of the worst hit countries by Iran this year, people said they still felt the psychological impact of the war. “There is still that traumatic effect ,” 21-year-old Fawaz told CNN. “When you hear the bombings, it’s kind of like you feel it in your hearts and it’s hard to sleep at night, especially when there are bombings outside.” “A lot of people have become used to it by now but it’s still very scary,” he added. Time Out Despite growing anxiety over the possible resumption of war, there has been a flurry of quiet diplomacy over the past week. US Vice President JD Vance sent Iran’s top security official Mohsen Rezaei a letter, which the Islamic Republic is reviewing, according to Iranian media. Trump has claimed that the letter was related to an Iranian request for medical supplies, but it has raised hopes a diplomatic breakthrough could still be possible. Iranian officials are in Qatar for talks, a Qatari official said. Qatar has played a prominent role mediating, but the official added there was no US delegation present Saturday. In stark contrast to Trump’s warnings, the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack told CNN’s Becky Anderson that he thinks there could be “dramatic steps” in the next two weeks “We’re close. I think we’re very close to a place where we can finally say: Let’s just have a time out,” he said, adding that it is, however, a “matter of trust and who goes first.” On Saturday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he would not characterize if progress had been made in the talks over the past 48 hours, but claimed that “if there is a diplomatic solution, we would be open to it.” Asked by CNN if the Trump administration has any time frame for progress in the talks before it would resume military action, Rubio said, “I don’t know if there’s a time frame,” noting that “it’s up to the president to make decisions with regards to those sorts of things.” “There are multiple talks. Talks have actually never stopped. There’s been active conversations going, both in some cases directly, but often through intermediaries,” he said at a press conference in Atlanta. “The president’s preference in any challenge around the world is to try to solve it diplomatically and peacefully, if possible,” Rubio said. “He recognizes there are some issues in the world that cannot be solved peacefully, unfortunately, sadly, but we would prefer to solve it in that manner.” Rubio said that any diplomatic solution “can’t be one that endangers our national security or one that doesn’t meet our core concerns,” particularly around Iran’s nuclear program. Iranian officials have said they’re open for diplomacy with the US, but they do not have trust that talks will stop military strikes, citing several past occasions when the Islamic Republic was struck during negotiations. And a central figure also warned that Iran was not ready to compromise. “Iran’s conditions have been repeatedly and clearly stated to the mediators,” said Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the Iranian parliamentary speaker who is leading negotiations with the US. “The carrot-and-stick approach has no effect on Iran. Progress can only be achieved once Iran’s seven conditions have been agreed upon.” CNN’S Jennifer Hansler contributed reporting. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/31/middleeast/gulf-braces-us-midterms-intl

item.title: Gov. Abbott's political machine faces a major test as Democrats gain ground in Texas
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
HOUSTON, Texas — On the first day of early voting in Texas, two weeks before the most consequential election Texas Republicans have faced in a generation, Greg Abbott addressed a sweaty crowd of hundreds of supporters packed inside an imitation saloon. The Texas governor pulled out a piece of paper from his pocket. “Steve Radack Community Center, 18650 Clay Road, Houston, 1.2 miles away,” he read, identifying the precinct’s nearest polling location. “Listen, I can roll over there in five minutes,” said Abbott, who uses a wheelchair, as the fawning audience laughed. Abbott was making a closing pitch to the Republican Party’s most fanatic supporters, many donning “Make America Texas” hats, who clapped loudly as he bragged about bringing 2.6 million jobs to Texas and booed at the mention of his “crazy" opponent, Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa. And they perked up when Abbott asked if they wanted to “be your own political power broker and make sure that you’re the one responsible for us winning.” That’s when the governor issued another set of directions: Download the Abbott Impact App, the engine of the massive turnout operation that has enabled the GOP to build tremendous power over Abbott’s nearly 12 years in Austin. Many in the audience dutifully complied. The app is the key to Abbott’s ability to maintain his grip on the most influential red state in the nation through his extensive data, polling and “get out the vote” operation — powerful tools that have not only allowed him to sail to reelection repeatedly but has cemented GOP control of every single statewide office. That could all change in a matter of days. Abbott expected to spend 2026 in legacy mode, cruising to a fourth term that would carry him into the post-Trump era as one of the most dominant state-level GOP figures in America, a kingmaker in a party looking for new heroes. Instead, he’s fighting a tougher-than-expected battle to retain his own seat, under weight from the unpopular war in Iran and rural blowback to data centers, Flock cameras and school vouchers. His longtime ticketmate, Attorney General Ken Paxton, is facing an even more arduous challenge in his attempt to keep the state’s U.S. Senate seat in Republican hands. A victory by Democrat James Talarico would crack a three-decade lockout from power in Texas for his party, and potentially redraw the national map ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Texas Republicans who have lost confidence in Paxton as a candidate, and are worried about the sour national mood more broadly, are now banking on Abbott’s finely tuned, expansive GOTV political machine to save the party. Ultimately, the election will reveal whether even the most powerful political force in Texas can fall — and determine what becomes of the Texas GOP if voters deliver a blow to the heart of American conservatism. “Paxton’s going to win the race,” Abbott told reporters in Austin in October as he kicked off a mad campaigning dash across the state, in response to being asked by POLITICO Magazine who gets the blame should Paxton lose. “So the real question is who gets the credit for it.” Not long ago there was a time when Abbott could clearly claim such credit. There’s arguably no Republican in America who has done more to nurture and benefit from the populist MAGA energy that President Donald Trump has unleashed over the past decade than Abbott. He has been able to navigate the yawning divisions between the two wings of the GOP by carefully riding the rise of the far right while also maintaining the respect of old school country club Republicans. That formula didn't work for Sen. John Cornyn, who found himself on the wrong side of MAGA a few too many times to maintain the fragile marriage of GOP factions and was ousted by Paxton in this year’s primary. Yet Abbott has deftly managed the party’s splintering, perhaps better than any other Republican whose rise pre-dated Trump. The question now is whether he can still motivate the base with the same intensity he’s done again and again. Even though most Texas Republicans — and many Democrats as well — quickly dismiss the scenario that Abbott himself could lose, public polling consistently shows Hinojosa within striking distance. Abbott has alienated rural voters over his staunch support for data centers and school vouchers , while his ties to megabillionaires have fueled a Democratic campaign that casts the election as a referendum on corruption as much as affordability. Meanwhile, some establishment Republicans have grown weary of the party’s fixation on culture-war battles that Abbott himself has helped stoke, particularly in an election where voters say they care more about the economy. It remains to be seen whether Abbott’s GOTV operation can surge turnout despite those headwinds. “He was the coattails for every cycle as governor,” said a senior Republican Texas official, granted anonymity to speak freely about the state’s dominant GOP leader. “He got people over the finish line in difficult House seats and Senate seats and congressional seats. He was the man.” This cycle, the official said, “Abbott has no coattails.” Texans of both parties say they’ve seen this scenario before: An abrasive, flamethrowing Republican is in the fight of his political life against a charismatic, rising-star Democrat who has reignited the party’s hopes of ending their decades-long losing streak in Texas by flipping a Senate seat. Faced with the limitations of his own ground game, the Republican leans on Abbott’s massive field operation to churn out votes, an organization powered by an army of thousands of volunteers and advanced data metrics. In 2018, Abbott’s operation helped Ted Cruz beat Beto O’Rourke by about 219,000 votes, running up the score in rural areas and turning out unreliable Republican voters. Cruz’s team saw the gap in the data: Abbott had a far broader coalition and a statewide field team that could help Republicans weather the unprecedented Democratic turnout O’Rourke was driving. The governor easily won his race by 13 points. “He’s feared because of a very effective organization,” said Bill Noble, a former senior adviser to Abbott’s predecessor, former Texas GOP Gov. Rick Perry. “It’s better to be on the side of having the governor endorsing you, and with that endorsement comes more than just a press release. Money’s made available, lists and resources are made available [and] delivering the vote after the endorsement.” Abbott’s hope is that the 2018 magic that saved Cruz can play out in the final years of the Trump era for Paxton, even with his party in transition. But the barriers facing the GOP — and Abbott himself — are far stronger this time around. Sure, Abbott can give Paxton a ground game. But can he turn Abbott voters into Paxton voters? And more to the point: Are there as many Abbott voters as there were in 2018? Meanwhile, after decades of being outgunned by Republicans, Democrats are working on building their own turnout machine. Brazoria County is the blueprint. Stretching from Houston to the Gulf Coast, this county has been run almost entirely by Republicans since the Republic of Texas was established in 1836. It’s the former political home base of the libertarian-leaning Republican Ron Paul and hotbed of the Tea Party movement before its reactionary politics went national in 2010. Therefore the odds are daunting for the small group of Democrats who, in 2025, devised a plan to mount a coordinated campaign within Brazoria County to assemble strength from the bottom up. The Brazoria project grew out of a statewide coordinated campaign launched this year by a coalition of Democratic groups who have invested $30 million in an effort to end the party’s 30-year drought in winning higher office. The experiment is targeting Brazoria this midterm and if successful, Democrats plan to replicate it across the state the next cycle. Texas Democrats have long yearned for year-round, state-wide campaign infrastructure. That burden typically falls on the Democrat at the top of the ticket to build out themselves, as in 2018 when O’Rourke created a massive, decentralized GOTV operation that relied on armies of volunteers. But after he lost, it evaporated. This cycle’s statewide coordinated campaign running in tandem with the Brazoria project intends to copy-and-paste that strategy but in a permanent way that will exist after the fumes of the 2026 election dissipate. Democrats believe the ingredients in Brazoria are all there, a microcosm of the story of Texas’ demographic growth over the last decade. Over the past 15 years, new residents from both inside and outside Texas have poured into the region, drawn by good schools, plentiful jobs and proximity to a major city — and by the promise of planting roots in the massive master-planned communities that have become a hallmark of Texas living. Brazoria’s growth is reshaping not just its suburbs but its demographics. Hispanic residents now make up about 32% of the county’s population, while Black residents account for roughly 18% and Asian residents nearly 9%. Those demographics work in Democrats’ favor: Enraged by ICE’s aggressive immigration enforcement under Trump, Latino voters are rapidly moving away from the GOP after a record number of them supported the president in 2024. But Texas Democrats are learning that demographics alone won’t deliver them power without some grit. The idea, Texas Majority PAC’s Katherine Fischer said, was to borrow from Republicans’ 1980s playbook: invest in rural, Democratic-leaning counties that were beginning to trend Republican — just the reverse. Brazoria caught their attention as they observed it shifting bluer cycle after cycle, although Democratic gains stalled slightly in 2024 when Trump won it by 20 points. They wanted to accelerate that shift, starting by recruiting a full slate of candidates for the first time. Republicans have so dominated the state’s politics that Democrats in the past didn’t even bother to field candidates in many down-ballot races. The Texas Democratic Party and Texas Majority PAC decided to fill every seat in Brazoria and partnered with County Democratic Chair Monica Morgan to make that happen. Those groups poured $450,000 into the project — hiring staff, paying for an office and covering the thousands of dollars in filing fees that dissuades potential candidates from making the leap. Candidates were then given one-on-one training through Texas Majority PAC, which provided campaign strategy, fundraising support, voter-data guidance and canvassing help. “[The PAC is] really pushing us in a healthy way to be successful,” said Becky Singleton, a Democrat running for county commissioner. “It took my own campaign to a whole new level.” The slate of Brazoria Democrats, who have become close friends throughout the cycle, got an early jolt of inspiration: In May, Democrat Quentin Wiltz flipped Brazoria’s biggest city of Pearland, winning by 263 votes in a city of about 130,000. For them it was a sign that Democrats had a chance to prevail, even in a county Trump carried by a wide margin. “We have millions of people in Texas who historically have been under-engaged,” Wiltz said. “When you give people a reason to participate and organize, and then when you have the resources to invest in them, you can reach them and you can see the change that’s possible.” Brazoria Republicans, in the face of a real opposition this year, are digging in. They’re even consolidating behind a deceased judicial candidate who died in September. Should the candidate win next week, the GOP-controlled board of county commissioners will appoint his replacement. (The Democrat in the race, Shenequa Harrison, makes the case that “if you vote for him, you literally you don't know who you're voting for.”) Democrats’ ambition now is to scale this model dramatically, with organizers saying they could recruit and support three times as many local candidates next cycle. “If we see that the experiment in Brazoria seems to be successful, we can then export that experiment to other counties across the state,” Fischer said, pointing to rapidly growing Kaufman County outside Dallas and the heavily Hispanic Rio Grande Valley as potential next targets. “We're not going to win overnight, but we will win one day, and we want to speed it up and make sure that we have good people in these seats when we do actually win.” Many Texas Republicans see Abbott’s GOTV dominance as an expression of his reputation as a hardworking overachiever with an intense obsession with detail. That reputation is in part a result of his biography: As a 26-year-old law firm associate studying for the bar, he was out for a jog when in a freak accident, a tree fell on him, leaving the lower half of his body paralyzed. The accident didn’t halt his meteoric rise from attorney to judge to state attorney general to governor. “He’s tenacious,” GOP state Sen. Paul Bettencourt said. “Incredibly disciplined,” said Republican state Rep. Greg Bonnen. “He has overcome a tremendous amount of adversity,” state Sen Phil King said. Abbott’s campaign knew that this would be a tough election year, so his aides adjusted their GOTV strategy. “We increased the targets and we increased the universe,” Dave Carney, Abbott’s top political adviser, told me. Rather than begin canvassing immediately after the primary, as it had during his previous reelection bid, the team held back its volunteers until the fall, betting that voter contact would be more effective once the race was on voters’ radar. Those volunteers — about 10,000 — have identified 3 million potential voters through the Abbott Impact App by uploading their contacts and matching them to voter files to confirm party affiliation and determine if they have voted. The app gamifies voter outreach, which occurs either through text or door knocks, and rewards top users with prizes like a Traeger grill, Dyson blowdryer or private tour of the governor’s mansion. “It’s basically a field operation on your phone,” Carney said. Abbott’s team insists they’re still focused on the governor’s goal of flipping seats in Harris County, which includes Houston and has a history of swinging between parties although it is currently Democratic-run. Abbott has devoted more than $30 million of his war chest to the effort. In 2024 Republicans successfully flipped several Harris judicial races and this year they’re eyeing races toward the top of the ballot like county judge — which would amount to an exceptional coup in a difficult year. “Any vote we pull out of Harris County is going to help the statewide ticket,” said Jessica Colon, Abbott’s senior adviser running the field operation in Harris County. “If it’s a voter numbers contact game, we’ve got ‘em smashed with that,” said Jeff MacGeorge, a district field director in Harris County, who said his team has sent more than 3.5 million texts to voters since the primary and 2,000 people in the county have downloaded the app. Republican state Rep. Gary Gates, who represents a district in the Houston area, said he opens the Abbott Impact App every Monday morning to see how many blocks the governor’s volunteers walked the weekend before, efforts the four-term Republican says he has never seen as organized or extensive. In one week in October the Abbott team knocked on more than 5,300 doors and completed 1,300 voter surveys in his Fort Bend County district, he said. But even with those efforts, Gates is pessimistic about how Republicans will fare next week given the negative national environment. After all, knocking on a voter’s door does not ensure they will show up at the polls for your side. “You just can’t go tick off and declare war on the Latinos and not have it come back and bite you in the rear end,” Cates said. “That’s going to have consequences.” Early vote returns signaled some warning signs for Republicans, with Democrats showing up in slightly higher numbers while rural voter turnout is lagging . Of course, those dynamics can quickly reverse, a possibility Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows is betting on, thanks largely to Abbott. “Many of them believe Election Day is the right day to vote,” he said. “So I expect us to have a huge Election Day for Republicans.” Burrows was doing his part, participating in a cross-state bus tour to mobilize Republicans: “It feels really good on the ground,” he told me. “It feels a whole lot better than what it sounds like on Twitter.” That confidence in the rural firewall is not shared among all Republicans, particularly with Abbott’s biggest detractors within the party. Former GOP state Rep. Glenn Rogers — whom Abbott successfully chased from office in his vendetta against lawmakers who opposed his school voucher push — said he’s had many conversations with Republicans in his small town of Graford indicating slipping support for the governor. Abbott’s efforts to attract data centers to Texas — which he dialed back following backlash — coupled with private school advocacy has alienated those supporters and promoted a “distrust” of him, Glenn said. A Republican defeat next week might trigger a recalibration within the party away from the culture wars and toward bread-and-butter economic issues, he said. “It’d be the best thing that could happen to them,” Glenn predicted. “I don’t see any change occurring in the Republican Party unless they get their ass whipped in November.” Back at the saloon in Houston, after Abbott concluded his remarks, a long line of fans waited to snap a photo with him before being rushed aside by an attentive staffer. Standing on the outskirts of the crowd stood a retired rancher from the border town of Brownsville, a longtime Republican in a family of other longtime Republicans who cast a ballot as soon as the polls opened. Asked about recent polls showing Hinojosa within a few points of Abbott, the rancher, who declined to share his name, dismissed them as “driven by Democrats.” And questioned about how he thinks his party will fare next week, he shrugged. “It’s Texas,” he said. item.title: GOP Rep. Salazar defends her Miami seat as immigration strains her voter coalition
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
M IAMI — For nearly an hour, dozens of the local Republican Party’s most loyal Colombian voters bided their time, piled into a conference room in a small hotel right off the airport near Miami Springs, surrounded by tables full of empanadas, tequeños and small Colombian flags. The event’s emcee, Weston City Commissioner Fabio Andrade, in town for the event, hyped up the crowd and warned of a “Machiavellian plan” by Democratic socialists to take over the U.S. He moved about the room, turning the mic to voters one by one. “ Porque apoyan a Maria Elvira?” he asked. Colombians of all ages easily made their case for why they support Maria Elvira Salazar. “ A favor de los inmigrantes!” “Defendie a los Latinos!” “ Se faja para el residente, y no para el partido.” She’s in favor of immigrants. She defends us Latinos. She works for the residents, not for the party. A salsa beat came in hot over the speakers. Right on cue, through a backdoor coming off the hotel parking lot, the congresswoman walked in. As if in complete coordination, the group lifted out of their seats and crowded her, whipping out cell phones to snap photos of her rapturous entrance. Sporting a white campaign shirt and white Golden Goose sneakers, her signature blowout slightly puffy from the excess humidity, Salazar was greeted like a celebrity. “I wish Washington would welcome me with this, and with this music!” she told the small crowd, taking her seat and signaling to one of her aides to grab her a water bottle. More members of her team funneled in, along with Toby, Salazar’s small but feisty King Charles Spaniel. The room quieted as she launched into a passionate defense of what has become her core policy proposal, the Dignity Act — the immigration reform measure that has put her at odds with President Donald Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement. Not long after, an older woman named Beatriz Parga, clad head to toe in red with a “TRUMP 2024” hat, stood and grabbed a mic: is the Dignity Act actually a mass amnesty? No, Salazar interjected quickly. It’s not. “Son ilegales y se quedaron, es verdad,” she said. They came illegally and they stayed. But, Salazar pleaded, “ vamos a hacer algo salomónico.” Let's do something Solomonic. “Trump could be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism,” Salazar told the crowd, a pitch she’s given so many times it’s become a cliché. For decades, Maria Elvira Salazar has been a rock star of the 305. A veteran of Spanish language television, her name has become synonymous with the Cuban American conservative tradition that provides one of the Republican Party’s most reliable bases of support. She’s a “Cuban Lauren Bacall,” as GOP strategist Giancarlo Sopo put it, so personally popular that in 2024 she won more votes in her Miami-based district than President Donald Trump himself. But in the second Trump era, the forced exodus of thousands of Venezuelans, Colombians, Nicaraguans and even Cubans has upended Miami’s immigrant community. It’s a policy that stands to unravel the broader GOP coalition that played a key role in Trump’s victory — and it’s threatening Salazar’s political survival. Interviews with more than two dozen lawmakers, lobbyists, former staffers, GOP operatives, Democratic organizers and Miami voters who know Salazar revealed the extent of the damage to her once-glittering political brand. Suddenly, she is as despised by some in her party as she is loved. Local Democrats loathe her, viewing Salazar as a hypocrite who has betrayed a vibrant city remade by an explosion of Latino culture and language. Those who support the administration’s mass deportation agenda view her as an existential threat to Trump’s restrictive immigration policies. Salazar’s predicament is unmistakable in the final days of the midterm campaign. She is facing what appear to be gale force Democratic winds while at the same time navigating the political hazards of one of the GOP’s most radioactive issues. She’s privately called James Blair, who heads Trump’s political operation, and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, to warn them that the party is at risk of losing Latino voters, she told POLITICO Magazine. “Right now in 2026, the polls are indicating that we may be losing some of that pot of gold if the Republican Party wants to stay in power and continue winning elections,” Salazar said. Neither Blair nor the White House responded to requests for comment. At the airport hotel event, as the crowd of Colombians swarmed Salazar after her remarks, squeezing up to the front to try and get a selfie with her, Parga held back. Parga told me she still supports Trump, and is a massive fan of Salazar. Yet when asked if she believes the congresswoman will win re-election in November, Parga shrugged. She wasn’t sure if voters would show up for her. “Los cubanos no están con ella,” Parga told me. The Cubans aren’t with her. But why? “Porque creen que ella no está con Trump,” she explained. They think she’s not with the president. With the clock ticking down toward Election Day, Salazar rolled up on a Wednesday in late September to a pale yellow warehouse off a back alley in Kendall — with a stack of papers and her dog Toby in tow — to record a podcast. The “Pichy Boys” are two content creators with over one million followers on Instagram. Though not explicitly a political show, the hosts are a mirror of Miami’s latest generation of Cubans, delivering their news and hot takes via Reels or TikToks. It’s a style of interview the congresswoman has done time and again on the trail this fall — usually friendly, and always with an important Cuban or Venezuelan or Colombian audience that she needs to turn out. Fixing her hair in the lens of the camera, Salazar appeared to be in her element. The studio had a great setup, she told the hosts. “That’s the most important part of a studio — lighting.” If there’s one thing to understand about Maria Salazar — core to the signature hair, the color-coordinated outfits, the news anchor posture — it’s that she was a fixture of local television for a very long time. That fact is relevant enough that Democrats chose their own veteran local TV personality to oppose her this year: Eliott Rodriguez, a former local news anchor for CBS, who is also Cuban American. Her media background places her squarely in a tradition of Spanish broadcasting that is the lifeblood of the Cuban exile community in South Florida. Since the first wave of migration from Cuba in the early 1960s — an influx which included Salazar’s own family — Cuban-led TV and radio has played an outsized role in Miami. First, it served as a source for exiles to understand what was happening to their families on the island, and for those on the island to get information they weren’t hearing from Fidel Castro’s revolutionary regime. It was resistance activism as much as it was news. Born in Miami’s Little Havana community just two years after Castro took control of the island, Salazar was part of the next generation of journalists. Univision, CNN en Español, Telemundo and then Mega TV — Salazar was everywhere. Over time, the whole Latino set of the city got to know “Maria Elvira.” “[Salazar] was one of the first people to actually do debate talk shows in Spanish on U.S. television,” said a person close to Salazar, granted anonymity to discuss private details. “She's pushy and she's extremely demanding, both with her producers and with her staff. She knows how to throw the zingers, and she's not afraid of controversy. She leans into it.” When Miami’s first Cuban representative in Congress, Republican Ileana Ros-Lehtinen, retired in 2018 — opening the seat for the first time in 20 years — Salazar seized the opportunity to leverage her celebrity. She was dragged under by that year’s blue wave, but in a rematch two years later with incumbent Democrat and former Cabinet secretary Donna Shalala, she took advantage of presidential year turnout — and the Cuban exile community’s affinity for Trump — to capture the seat. Notably, Salazar ran ahead of Trump’s performance in her congressional district. “She was having nightly Zoom shows on Facebook Live with thousands of people, talking about the pandemic,” one of her former campaign staffers said. “The cars would stop in the middle of the street and honk and wave her down,” when they saw her on the trail. “It all goes back to the fact that she is a journalist and she understands TV extremely well.” It “turned out to be the biggest upset in the country in 2020, because the GOP never really thought, including [former Speaker] Kevin McCarthy, that I could defeat the longest serving member of the Clinton administration with no money from the GOP,” Salazar said. “So yeah, miracles happen.” From the moment she took her oath in the Capitol, Salazar wanted to “speak and talk and live and walk immigration,” she said in an interview between meetings this week. It formed the crux of her character on the Hill. In her 2025 book, Dignity Not Citizenship: The Truth About Immigration No One Is Telling You , she described herself as a freshman “with a mission, not to mention a minority woman with a Sofia Vergara accent, who spoke loudly and waved her arms around to drive home a point.” She quickly made allies of her fellow Miami Cuban lawmakers. “There is a difference between, you know, being a journalist and getting into this crazy process,” Republican Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart said. “Her work ethic is just outstanding,” he added, calling Salazar “exceedingly intense.” The expansive laws crafted to facilitate the settling of Cubans in the U.S. have always made them an exception among immigrant groups. Yet Salazar was convinced that the next wave of Latinos that came flocking to South Florida in the 2000’s weren’t as fortunate. So she formed the beginnings of a framework that could legalize the swaths of immigrants who had moved without papers to the U.S. decades ago, but had never gotten status. She called it the Dignity Plan. Together with Democratic Rep. Veronica Escobar of Texas, she pushed to establish a new “dignity” status for immigrants who’d been living in the U.S. for years, where they would never be eligible for a green card and would agree to pay thousands of dollars in fines. Salazar argues that the bill would clear backlogs in the courts, help immigrants to fill gaps in the workforce and secure the Southern border. Escobar remembers that when they first met, she was “not a fan” of Salazar. “She said, ‘You need to do something about immigration,’ and just started laying into me. And I remember just thinking, ‘Who the hell does she think she is to walk up and confront me in this way?’” Escobar said. But the Texas Democrat also acknowledged that only Salazar came to mind when she looked for a Republican to partner with on a bipartisan immigration proposal. “She has determination that is almost superhuman,” Escobar said. “She is different from a number of legislators that I've worked with over the years, in that respect that she is almost relentless to a point of obsession.” But the latter years of the Biden administration saw an immigration crisis that completely shifted the calculus in Congress. A constant stream of headlines about caravans of immigrants entering through the Southern border inflamed a Republican Party that already viewed the president as dangerously lax on immigration policy. To them, Salazar’s bill amounted to a “mass amnesty” that would worsen an already chaotic situation on the border. And with the GOP taking control of the House in 2023, it was a complete nonstarter. It wasn’t just Salazar’s Republican colleagues in Washington who were enraged by the idea of letting in more immigrants. Back in Miami, Cuban Republicans — the oldest of whom had spent half their lives in the U.S., by that point — were also convinced the influx had to stop. Nicaraguan, Colombian and Venezuelan immigrants, the ones who had become U.S. citizens, were thinking the same thing. Those frustrations helped power Trump, who was promising the “largest deportation program of criminals” in American history, to a sweeping victory in Miami-Dade County in 2024. More than two-thirds of Cubans voted for him. Salazar, who had campaigned against the chaos at the border and messaged her immigration reform proposal as a tool for shutting the border, won re-election by an even greater margin — 20 points. Just two years later, however, Miami — and Salazar’s winning coalition — is at risk of fracturing. Away from the loud, music-filled storefronts of Little Havana’s Calle Ocho , the tourists looking for coffee and the older Cubans loyal to their game tables at Domino Park, the surrounding neighborhood remains one of the last real working or middle class enclaves of Salazar’s district. And amid relics of Spanish architecture and sprawling murals of the Cuban flag, the streets are largely quiet these days. Almost everyone has a story of someone they know who left out of fear of ICE. Ask your Uber driver to take you to Little Havana, or to Doral, a small immigrant-dominated city outside Salazar’s district known as Doral- zuela , and many will flat out tell you no. They can’t risk being stopped in their car there. It’s a level of fear, of frustration, of wariness, that’s unlike anything residents have experienced here — I grew up here, and felt it myself when I returned to report for this story. “They’re treating everyone like criminals, but we built Miami,” Martha Cabrera, a Cuban canvasser with the UNITE Here local 355 chapter, told me while knocking doors. I told her that Salazar was born in this neighborhood. “It seems like she forgot,” responded Martha, who was doorbelling for an independent offshoot that has backed Eliott Rodriguez. The shadow cast by federal immigration enforcement and the detention sweeps has been impossible to avoid. As mass ICE detentions swept the country in 2025 and plunged major cities into protest, Miami registered the highest number of ICE arrests of any field office. That included Cubans — who for much of Miami’s recent history were thought to be untouchable. The converging factors of existing city agreements to cooperate with ICE enforcement, and the sudden termination of status for hundreds of thousands of immigrants, living and working in Miami legally under Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designation, created a perfect storm for removals. Nearby loomed the makeshift detention center established by Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis. Dubbed “Alligator Alcatraz” for its location near the Everglades, the facility was widely condemned for inhumane detention conditions until it was shut down in June. “The word is decepcionado, ” explained Ana Sofia Pelaez, a local activist and executive director of the Miami Freedom Project, when asked how Latino voters felt about the detention policies. “In English it can mean you were deceived or you were just disappointed.” In Spanish, it means both. In D.C., Salazar started sounding the alarm about what she was hearing back home. Latino voters were angry, she told her colleagues. The indiscriminate enforcement wasn’t what they voted for. Her Miami Republican colleagues, from Diaz-Balart and Carlos Gimenez to local Republicans, raised the same red flags. She warned GOP leadership that if the enforcement continued, they would lose Latino voters in the midterms. “That's a mistake that is going to cost us dearly, and I've been telling my Trump administration. I've been telling ICE,” she told reporters in July. She explained to fellow House Republicans that, thanks to Trump, the Southern border was now closed. She saw an opening for the Dignity Act, which she had re-introduced along with Escobar in 2025. “I'm trying to make the GOP the party that will send the message to the Hispanics that they're welcomed and that they have the same values that are entrenched in the Republican Party: God-fearing, law-abiding, tax-paying, good people, hard workers,” Salazar said. “They are here, so let's just give them dignity so they can stay.” Instead, she found herself in what she called a “two-front war”: Democrats wouldn’t work with her without the promise of a path to citizenship, and many Republicans simply rejected her plan outright. In fact, top administration allies, key Trump confidants and Salazar’s own GOP colleagues on the Hill lead the charge against the measure. “The Dignity Act is mass amnesty and would constitute a terrible betrayal of our voters,” Republican Rep. Brandon Gill of Texas, one of the bill’s biggest critics, wrote on X . One of her Florida delegation colleagues, Republican Rep. Randy Fine, wrote on X that it “should never see the light of day” in the House. Several far-right advocates came together to form a Mass Deportation Coalition at the height of the backlash, and some formed a PAC to specifically attack “pro-amnesty” candidates who backed the Dignity Act . The congresswoman is “first and foremost, an ethno-lobbyist,” said Mike Howell of the Mass Deportation Coalition. “What are you doing here, Maria Salazar? Go join the other party,” he added. “How can the president endorse somebody who is boldly opposing his central thesis?” Mark Krikorian, executive director of the right-leaning Center for Immigration Studies, called the proposal “so preposterous” that the party shouldn’t even engage with it. Even if it was viable, Krikorian said, Salazar should not be the face of it because “she’s incredibly obnoxious and aggressive, and turns off people even on our own side.” Salazar said she received death threats for her departure from MAGA orthodoxy. There were calls for her to be primaried. “I don't want the Republicans to lose the House, but at this point in time, like, what's the difference between Maria Salazar and a Democrat?” Laura Loomer told POLITICO back in April. Democrats have been just as hard on her, for voting along party lines to allocate billions of dollars to the agency behind the ICE detention sweeps, the Homeland Security Department. “Maybe at one time she was known as a tough journalist and someone who could be trusted, but by now people know her as a politician who cannot be trusted and who doesn't tell the truth,” Rodriguez, Salazar’s Democratic opponent, told POLITICO Magazine. “She votes with MAGA all the time, and they're not fooled by it.” Caught between two pincers, Salazar went back to her roots in September: She got on TV. This time, with a message for Trump himself. Standing in front of the White House, speaking directly to the camera, Salazar told the president that “some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far.” The campaign ad went on: “Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy … The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.” In Miami, almost no one was surprised by the spot. But back in Washington, it hit like a political earthquake, a rare rebuke of a president who tolerates no dissent from the party line. The video went viral, racking up millions of views. “I wanted him to hear directly from me,” Salazar said. “[I was] not attacking him. I was forewarning him.” “He's a construction and hospitality guy. He's a businessman. He is the one to fix this 40-year problem,” she added. To the far-right — the “America First” believers in Trump’s campaign promises — her position had already represented an “existential threat” to the future of the Republican Party. But the ad? Name-checking the president? Right in front of the White House? It crossed a line. Angry callers inundated Miami’s Cuban radio shows, phoning in to say Salazar went too far. Ninoska Pérez Castellón, host at “La Poderosa” and one of the giants of the Cuban conservative airwaves, was among the radio hosts fielding the calls. Whoever wrote the ad, she said, did Salazar “un gran mal” — a disservice. “She could have said the same thing without using the language that she used,” Pérez Castellón said. “The word she used is ‘betrayed.’ That [Trump] ‘betrayed’ us. I don’t know if I agree.” At first, Trump showed Salazar a little grace. Rather than revoke his endorsement, he told reporters she was a “nice person” who “got a little bit soft on the border.” Then he had a change of heart. He re-shared a series of Truth Social posts attacking her, and in some cases, calling for her replacement. Sitting at the center of a long table, flanked by the Republican mayors from the southern neighborhoods of her district, Salazar held court on a recent October morning. Hundreds of attendees packed the meeting, from prominent Miami industry reps to regular constituents, all gathered at 7:30 am to meet her at Casa Cuba, a classic South Miami spot. Grant Miller of Miami Community Newspapers, which hosted the breakfast for Salazar, invited the congresswoman up to the small stage and got down on one knee to hold her stack of papers, not long after joking he would marry her. Donning bright red reading glasses, Salazar without delay launched into her immigration pitch. “I do believe Trump will sign immigration reform law, and it will be Dignity,” she told the room. “Once the Dignity Act passes, I will have done my job.” Even in the final stretch of an increasingly competitive — and contentious — race, Salazar has not backed down from the position that has made her a pariah to many in her party. It’s made her a test case for whether a Republican can win a majority Latino district in the era of mass deportation. Outside Casa Cuba, sitting at a tiled table after the breakfast, Ramona Tumon and Mirla Loredo lamented they weren’t able to grab a photo with the congresswoman. The pair of friends, both Cuban, moved to Miami in the late 60’s. Loredo told me in no uncertain terms: she’s not a fan of the Dignity Act and she didn’t like Salazar’s ad. Tumon, however, did support the proposal. She tried to convince Loredo to no avail. Both already voted Republican up and down the ballot, including for Salazar. Why vote for Salazar, I asked Loredo, if you disagree with her signature policy proposal? She said she didn’t want the GOP to lose the House. Cuban Republicans may be angry with Salazar, Loredo said, but they have to vote GOP in spite of it. “ No les queda más remedio,” she said. “They don’t have another choice.” “ Tienen que votar por ella, sino nos toca el otro,” Loredo added. “They have to vote for her, or else we get the other guy,” referring to Rodriguez. Salazar remains a slight favorite to win. She has significantly outspent Rodriguez, who has gone through the race without any ads on broadcast TV. He’s the beneficiary of a late infusion of support from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and an 11th hour spend by the House Majority PAC, but the GOP has a voter registration edge of about 45,000 voters, according to Florida International University’s Eduardo Gamarra. The latest FIU Cuba poll , which has been surveying the community for years, found that 76% of respondents disapprove of the administration’s immigration crackdown on Cuban nationals — but 68% of Cubans still plan to vote for the GOP candidate in their district next week. Yet with significant headwinds buffeting the Republican Party, and Trump’s approval rating plummeting, GOP turnout is by no means guaranteed — in Miami or anywhere else. “They're not enthusiastic about going out to the polls,” Gamarra said. For many Latino Republicans, “they're not switching parties, and they're just simply not going to show up.” If Republicans do show up on Election Day, said Venezuelan activist Adelys Ferro of Latino Victory, it may be due to the deep loyalty to MAGA that still thrives in Salazar’s Cuban base, an affinity rooted in Trump’s anti-socialist and law-and-order messaging. “If she loses,” Ferro argued, “it’s on her.” Should Salazar win on Tuesday, her problems will be far from over. She’ll likely return to Washington as a member of the House minority. A disproportionate number of her Republican Dignity Act co-sponsors may not survive their own re-elections. Trump’s final two years have set a hard deadline to make good on Salazar’s repeated assurances that he’ll sign sweeping immigration reform, but he’s given no indication to date that he’s willing to buck the MAGA base on the issue. Salazar has demurred from making any grand predictions about what voters will do on Nov. 3. “I know District Number 27 probably better than anybody,” she told reporters after the Casa Cuba event, as a line of constituents formed to get photos with her. “If they think that I've done a good job, they'll bring me back, regardless of the political affiliation.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/31/trumps-ice-crackdown-broke-miami-will-it-tank-this-cuban-republicans-campaign-01140214

item.title: Democratic candidates criticize Biden's border record in push to win swing voters
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
James Talarico; Adam Hamilton; Paige Cognetti. (USA Today Network; Reuters; Getty) WASHINGTON — Democratic candidates in 2026 battleground races are directly criticizing Joe Biden’s handling of border security when he was president, seeking to neutralize a political vulnerability and signaling a new path for the party on the thorny issue. Candidates are throwing the ex-president under the bus on border policy in key states that will decide control of the Senate and some battleground House races across the country. “I called out Joe Biden for failing us on the border,” Texas’ Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico says in a recent ad airing in the closing stretch of his neck-and-neck race against Republican Ken Paxton. He also criticized Biden in July for having “failed us on our southern border” as he rolled out his own border security plan . He’s not alone. In Kansas, a longtime Republican stronghold, Democrat Adam Hamilton criticized Biden in a recent debate with Republican Sen. Roger Marshall. “I want to be crystal clear, first of all: Immigration at the border under Biden was a disaster. That is how we ended up where we are today,” he said. “Second, what we did in response to that has been a disaster for people across the state of Kansas.” Hamilton, like other Democrats in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, paired their critique of Biden with criticism that the current president has gone too far on enforcement. Polls show many Americans have soured on Trump’s handling of the issue in the wake of immigration officers fatally shooting two Americans in Minnesota and one in Maine this year. Still, the comments reflect a recognition that the issue of border security remains a vulnerability for Democrats as Republicans continue to accuse them of promoting “open borders” in a bid to mobilize their base and win swing voters. Biden’s ratings on the issue tanked amid a surge in migrant crossings during his presidency, which Trump successfully weaponized in 2024. Entering office in 2021, Biden inherited a Covid-era migration surge that intensified in the United States after he made good on his pledge to roll back Trump-era policies and restrictions, allowing more asylum-seekers to stay in the country as their cases were being considered. The collective result was a huge spike in border crossings that became associated with the Biden presidency and brought down his approval ratings. Even as Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 38% , polls show border security continues to be one of his highest-polling issues, although that number has fallen from the highs of his early second term. “The Biden administration failed at the border,” Democratic House candidate Paige Cognetti said at a debate Thursday night. Cognetti, who is vying to unseat Rep. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., in a highly competitive Scranton-area working-class district, later added: “The Biden administration did fail. We need to make sure that the border is secure. It’s a good thing that it is. We do need to make sure that the pathways to citizenship are there.” In South Carolina, Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews said in a debate, “Democrats have failed on the border.” Democratic pollster Celinda Lake said it’s “very smart” for candidates to distance themselves from Biden and that “there’s nobody contesting that interpretation” that he blundered on the border. In the 2024 election, “immigration was playing a major, major role, and it was energizing Republicans. And it was the best issue among swing voters for Republicans,” she said. “ICE has gone too far, and that has backfired now.” She added that the “best messaging” on immigration is “some control for the border plus a humanitarian process for immigration.” Iowa’s Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek traveled more than 800 miles to Laredo, Texas, to film an ad at the border touting his support for tougher enforcement. “I came to the border to meet firsthand with the people who work to keep it secure. What happens down here affects us up in Iowa, so we’ve got to address it,” Turek says in the ad . “I voted with Republicans to allow law enforcement to arrest and deport criminals.” Weeks earlier, he released another ad speaking to Iowans and vowing that he would “work with anyone” to fix immigration — “including President Trump, to secure the border.” Closer to the border, Democrat Johnny Garcia is trying to win Texas’ redrawn and Republican-friendly 35th Congressional District against GOP nominee Carlos De La Cruz. Garcia criticized Trump’s ICE raids as detrimental to the economy. But at a recent forum , he also blamed Biden’s policies for failures at the border and referred to a fatal smuggling conspiracy in 2022 that led to the deaths of dozens of people. “We’ve also gotten to see, unfortunately, how Biden got it wrong on the border,” Garcia said. “I’ll admit that every single day. We got to see one of the largest migrant fatalities in this district in south San Antonio, with 53 migrants that were locked in a trailer.” “So we can’t afford to just turn a blind eye to our border,” he added. “But at the same time, we can’t turn a blind eye to what we’re seeing happening on our streets.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/2026-democratic-candidates-throw-joe-biden-bus-border-security-rcna603228

item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The 2026 midterm elections are just three days away. So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to geek out over some cold, hard data. The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. And they have been wrong before . Yet time is running out — and the stakes in November couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too. The state-by-state midterm landscape is reaching its final form — and some clear polling trends have emerged. Here are the numbers to watch as Election Day nears. The generic congressional ballot Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds). You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading. History is helpful here, courtesy of the RealClear Politics polling average : At this point in 2022 — after more than a year and a half of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Republicans had a small but significant lead (2.7 percentage points) on the generic ballot. On Election Day, the GOP translated its final polling lead of 3 percentage points into nine seats — enough to flip the House. At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 7.2 points on the generic ballot. Three days later, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But with three days to go, voters had clearly broken against Democrats. In 2014, a Republican polling lead of 2.5 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House; in 2010, those numbers were 6.5 points and 63 seats, respectively. So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot — nearly 9 percentage points , on average. And that margin has held steady over the last month. Democrats might not reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with . But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House. Advantage? Democrats. 12 specific Senate races National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible. In the states where Dems are playing defense — Michigan, Georgia, New Hampshire — their leads are solidifying; meanwhile, red states such as Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and South Carolina seem increasingly competitive. That's a 45-point gap. In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection. Advantage? Democrats. item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Kai Pfaffenbach, Tilman Blasshofer and Miranda Murray FRANKFURT/BERLIN, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Hooded rioters looted stores in Frankfurt late on Saturday after tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across Germany's biggest cities to demand better education and lower living costs. The protests followed a wave ‌of Gen Z-led demonstrations across Europe this year. In Serbia, student-led activism helped unseat the country's longtime leader at the ballot box, while protests in ‌France have descended into rioting and looting. The German protests organised by the campaign group "Gen Z regelt" — "Gen Z takes charge" in German — took place in 34 cities including Berlin, Frankfurt and Munich. The group says ​it opposes compulsory military service and wants greater investment in education as many young Germans struggle with rising costs. In Frankfurt, Germany's financial hub, at least two stores were looted as protests turned violent, with several more damaged and police trying to get the situation under control, according to a Reuters witness. "Violent disturbances are continuing," Frankfurt police said on X. "In the city centre, windows have been smashed at several shops. Molotov cocktails are also being thrown at the emergency services. We urge all bystanders to avoid the city centre ‌or to leave the area." Official numbers on Saturday afternoon ⁠suggested turnout was below the 182,000 participants that organisers initially expected. Police in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, half the roughly 36,000 on the organisers' website. German authorities said Saturday's demonstrations, which coincide with Halloween festivities, had been largely peaceful, but ⁠warned of attempts by extremist groups to exploit the movement. In Hamburg, some barricades had been set on fire. "We are here today to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion," Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said in Berlin on Saturday. "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory ​military ​service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden." LUXURY SHOPS BOARD UP ​WINDOWS Parts of Germany's far-left extremist scene and some groups linked ‌to foreign extremist movements have joined efforts to mobilise support, according to the federal interior ministry. "We all have those images from France in our minds — looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers," said Roman Poseck, interior minister for the state of Hesse, whose capital is Germany's financial hub, Frankfurt. "France must not be held up as a model in this regard." Some businesses across German cities boarded up windows and planned early closures ahead of the demonstrations due to concerns over possible unrest, including along Berlin's luxury Kurfuerstendamm shopping boulevard. Organisers have focused on what they see as the growing pressure on younger generations in Europe's largest economy. "The government has offered no ‌response to our concerns other than to continue making cuts and piling further burdens upon ​us," said Steve, an 18-year-old due to speak at a rally in Munich, addressing Chancellor Friedrich Merz. "We ​will continue to exercise our fundamental right to assemble until you stop ​ignoring us." Germany has struggled to revive economic growth. The country also faces growing pressure on pensions and public services as baby boomers ‌retire and the working-age population shrinks. Questions have been raised about who ​is driving the campaign and whether it ​is genuinely youth-led, given the broad mix of political and civil society groups involved. Germany's national school student umbrella organisation, BSK, has distanced itself from the initiative and plans to hold a separate day of protest on November 20. Sean Baker, a student at the Technical University of Berlin, said he would join ​the protests on Saturday to call attention to the ‌poor state of buildings on campus. "When you go inside and enter the rooms, it looks like an abandoned building," he told Reuters. "Yet this is ​where we're expected to study on a regular basis." item.title: What changes when the clocks fall back this weekend
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Millions of Americans will gain an hour of sleep this weekend when the twice-a-year time change commonly known as daylight savings ends for 2026. Most of the U.S. will "fall back" an hour when the clocks change at 2 a.m. on Sunday. Here's what to know about what's formally known as daylight saving time as it ends for the year: What is daylight saving time, and why do we have it? Daylight saving time is the period during the year, from March to early November, when the majority of the U.S. operates one hour ahead of standard time. The move effectively "saves" an hour of daylight from the morning and adds it to the evening during the spring and summer months when the days are the longest. In the fall and winter months, when the days are shorter, the U.S. returns to standard time, with daylight coming earlier in the morning. For example, in Boston on Saturday, before the time change, the sun will rise at 7:16 a.m. and set at 5:39 p.m., according to the National Weather Service . On Sunday, back on standard time, sunrise will be at 6:17 a.m. and sunset will be at 4:37 p.m. The U.S. first adopted daylight saving time in 1918 during World War I as an effort to conserve fuel after Europe implemented its own time change, according to the Congressional Research Service . After the war, Congress repealed the clock switch but gave states the option to continue observing it. During World War II and the 1970s energy crisis, Congress brought year-round daylight saving time to the U.S., again with the goal of reducing energy consumption. These experiments didn't last long. After the war, the U.S. let states and municipalities decide for themselves if they wanted to keep daylight saving time and when to observe it. (Congress didn't establish a uniform start and end for the time change until 1966.) In the '70s, continuous daylight saving time was stopped before reaching the 10-month mark. Will the U.S. move to year-round daylight saving time? Earlier this year, legislation to once again make daylight saving time last all year long cleared a major hurdle in Congress. The bill, called the Sunshine Protection Act, passed the House in July and went to the Senate . The legislation would also let states opt out of daylight saving time altogether before the law takes effect. President Trump, who supports the bill, accused a fellow Republican, Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, of holding up the legislation . Mr. Trump even posted to social media what he said was Cotton's cellphone number and urged people to call the senator to express their support for the measure. In response, Cotton noted Congress has tried permanent daylight saving time before, only to go back to the twice-yearly time change "once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter." There is a ticking clock for the Senate to take action on the bill. The legislation and any other bills awaiting approval in Congress are set to expire in early January when the new class of lawmakers elected in Tuesday's midterm elections takes office. If the bill does die, the effort to change daylight saving time will have to start over and be approved by the House and the Senate before it can go to the president. Did the time change today? The time won't change until Sunday. For 2026, the end of daylight saving time comes during the overnight hours after Halloween, giving revelers an extra hour of enjoying late-night costume parties — or an extra hour of sleep to recover from their fun. But for parents of young children, the time change can be more of a trick and less of a treat, potentially disrupting their kids' sleep schedules until they adjust. What day and time does daylight saving time end in November 2026? Daylight saving time officially ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, Nov. 1. Americans have been "falling back" on the first Sunday of November since 2007, when the most recent changes to daylight saving time took effect . A 2005 law moved the end date from the last Sunday of October. Do we lose or gain an hour when daylight saving time ends? Most Americans will gain an hour when daylight saving time ends, making up for the hour they lost when the clocks "sprang forward" in March. When will daylight saving time start again in 2027? Daylight saving time is set to begin in 2027 on Sunday, March 14, at 2 a.m. local time. The time change starts on the second Sunday of March, which falls on such a late date next year because the month starts on a Monday. In 2026, daylight saving time started on March 8 . The start date was also changed in 2007 to extend the length of daylight saving time, which previously began on the first Sunday of April. Which states don't do daylight saving time? Daylight saving time is observed in every state except for Hawaii and most of Arizona . The Navajo Nation, which is located in part of Arizona, observes the time change to stay on the same time as their communities in the neighboring states of New Mexico and Utah, according to the tribe . The U.S. territories of American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands also don't observe daylight saving time. Will my phone change for daylight saving time automatically? Phones should change overnight to display the correct time if they're set to update automatically. Apple , Google and Samsung have support pages with instructions for changing the clocks on their devices. Carriers like Simple Mobile and Straight Talk have also posted steps online for checking the settings on other phones. item.title: El-Sayed drops former primary rival from Michigan event days before election
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) told Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), his once primary opponent, to stay away from his campaign events and disinvited her from a planned appearance on Sunday, a source familiar confirmed to NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcasting partner. The source said El-Sayed does not want the ongoing fight with Stevens to distract from the issues in the final days of his hard-fought Senate campaign. A spokesperson for Stevens did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment. El-Sayed was set to appear alongside Stevens and Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.) at a church in Detroit, a show of unity despite some harsh words exchanged between the two candidates throughout the week. Stevens released a statement saying she had accepted Clyburn’s invitation to appear alongside El-Sayed, but still criticized the Senate nominee for not condemning an ad that appeared to blame Israel for high grocery prices. “The ad did not invent its argument; it dramatized one Dr. El-Sayed has made in his own words throughout this campaign: that Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, healthcare, and child care,” Stevens said in her statement. “I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well.” The ad was run digitally and was bought by an outside progressive group, not El-Sayed’s campaign. El-Sayed shot back in a statement on Friday, saying Stevens is focused on rehashing their August primary, which he narrowly won. “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics,” El-Sayed said in a statement posted to the social platform X. Support for Israel was a major issue in the Democratic primary. Stevens was backed by millions in funds from pro-Israel lobbying groups, which El-Sayed criticized her for. The Democratic Senate nominee is critical of Israel and has called for the U.S. to stop sending aid to the country. Since the primary, courting Jewish voters has been a hurdle for El-Sayed. His Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has worked to earn the support of disaffected Democrats, including those who are Jewish.
